title: Aeneas Indiges
source: P. Ovidius Naso, Metamorphoses, ed. Hugo Magnus (Gotha: F.A. Perthes), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-latinLit phi0959.phi006.perseus-lat2, sha256 8719b7d375018d4f. Collated against The Latin Library (cltk mirror) as a disagreement detector only. Original spelling kept. Pronunciation convention: reconstructed Classical (restored) Latin, applied consistently. All translations were made fresh from the Latin for Lectorium.
about: Aeneas' own valour has worn the gods down, Juno included, and with the fortunes of his son Iulus secure he is ripe for heaven. Venus goes to her father Jupiter with her arms round his neck and asks a godhead for Aeneas, however small a one, on the ground that a single journey through the kingdom of the dead is enough for any man. Jupiter grants it in front of the assenting gods; Venus then rides her doves to the Latian coast and has the river Numicius wash out of Aeneas everything in him liable to death, anoints what is left, and the Roman people receive him under the cult title Indiges. The whole part is built on a vocabulary of petition and grant — ambierat, petis, des, cape — and it closes Ovid's compressed retelling of the Aeneas story.

sentences.t:
Iamque deos omnes ipsamque Aeneia virtus
Iunonem veteres finire coegerat iras,
cum, bene fundatis opibus crescentis Iuli,
tempestivus erat caelo Cythereius heros:
sentences.l: And by now Aenean valour had compelled all the gods, and Juno herself, to finish their old angers, when — the resources of the growing Iulus being well founded — the Cytherean hero was ripe for heaven:
sentences.i: By now the valour Aeneas had shown had forced all the gods, and Juno herself, to have done with their old anger; and now that the fortunes of the growing Iulus stood on firm foundations, the hero born of Venus was ripe for heaven:
sentences.n: Iamque … cum is the “inverted” cum: the main event of the sentence arrives in the cum clause, so the shape is “and by now X had happened, when Y”. Aeneia is an adjective, “Aenean”, not a genitive — the quality does the compelling and the man is named only through it. bene fundatis opibus is an ablative absolute, a self-contained “with X done” phrase where English wants a clause. Iulus is Ascanius, Aeneas' son, and the name is three syllables, I-u-li, which is what the line needs to scan. Cythereius heros is Aeneas by his mother: Venus came ashore at Cythera. tempestivus, “ripe, in season”, takes the dative caelo — ripe for heaven, that is, ready to be made a god.

sentences.t:
ambieratque Venus superos, colloque parentis
circumfusa sui “numquam mihi” dixerat “ullo
tempore dure pater, nunc sis mitissimus, opto,
sentences.l: and Venus had canvassed the gods above, and, having poured herself about the neck of her own parent, had said, “Father never harsh to me at any time, now be most gentle, I pray,
sentences.i: and Venus had gone round the gods above, and with her arms flung about her father's neck she had said, “You have never been harsh to me at any hour, father — now, I beg, be gentler than ever,
sentences.n: ambio is the canvasser's word — to go round soliciting votes — and Venus works the assembly before she works her father. circumfusa is a participle used reflexively, a “middle”: “having poured herself around”, not “having been poured”, with collo as its dative and the genitive parentis sui, “of her own parent”, hanging on that. dure pater is a vocative, and numquam … ullo tempore piles a negative on an “any” to reinforce rather than cancel it: “never at any time”. sis is the subjunctive of the wish, governed by opto at the end of the line. The speech-verb dixerat sits inside the quoted words, which is why Magnus's quotation marks open twice. This unit is cut at a comma: the Latin period runs from 585 to the colon at 590 with no internal stop to cut at.

sentences.t:
Aeneaeque meo, qui te de sanguine nostro
fecit avum, quamvis parvum des, optime, numen,
dummodo des aliquod:
sentences.l: and to my Aeneas, who out of our blood made you a grandfather, grant a godhead, however small, O best one, provided only that you grant some:
sentences.i: and give my Aeneas — who made you a grandfather out of our own blood — some divinity, however small, best of fathers; only let there be some:
sentences.n: des is a second subjunctive still governed by opto in 587 — Venus is going on saying “I pray that …” — though in English it comes out as the near-command it amounts to. quamvis parvum … numen is concessive, “a godhead, however small”, and dummodo des aliquod is a proviso clause with its own subjunctive: she gives away the size in advance and holds only to the fact. de sanguine nostro is literal family reckoning — Venus is Jupiter's daughter, so Aeneas' birth made Jupiter a grandfather. optime is a vocative addressed to Jupiter, standing between the adjective parvum and the noun numen it belongs to.

sentences.t:
satis est inamabile regnum
adspexisse semel, Stygios semel isse per amnes.”
sentences.l: it is enough to have looked upon the unlovely kingdom once, to have gone once through the Stygian streams.”
sentences.i: it is enough to have set eyes on that unlovable realm once, and passed once through the streams of Styx.”
sentences.n: Two perfect infinitives stand as the subject of satis est: “to have looked … is enough”. inamabile regnum is the kingdom of the dead, and Venus is arguing from Aeneas' own descent to it: a man who has made that journey once should not be left mortal and have to make it twice. semel is repeated in both halves of 591, the second time pushed inside its phrase (Stygios semel isse). adspexisse keeps the edition's adsp- spelling; isse is the contracted form of ivisse.

sentences.t:
Adsensere dei, nec coniunx regia vultus
immotos tenuit placatoque adnuit ore;
sentences.l: The gods assented, nor did the royal consort keep her features unmoved, and she nodded with a face made calm;
sentences.i: The gods gave their assent, and the queen his wife did not hold her face unmoved: she nodded, her look appeased;
sentences.n: Adsensere is the poetic third-plural perfect, -ere for -erunt — you will meet this ending constantly in verse; read it as “they assented”, never as an infinitive. coniunx regia is Juno, named only by her marriage, and she is the “Juno herself” whose old angers 582 said had been worn down. The negative is understatement for its opposite: “did not keep her features unmoved” means she softened. placato … ore is an ablative of manner wrapped round adnuit.

sentences.t:
tum pater “estis” ait “caelesti numine digni,
quaeque petis, pro quoque petis:
sentences.l: then the father says, “You are worthy of heavenly godhead, both you who ask and he for whom you ask:
sentences.i: then her father says, “You are both worthy of a godhead in heaven — you who ask, and the one you ask for:
sentences.n: estis is plural: Jupiter answers Venus and Aeneas in one breath, and the two clauses that follow unpack the plural — quae petis, “(you) who ask”, feminine, and pro quo petis, “(he) for whom you ask”. Beware the quoque trap here: pro quoque is pro quo-que, “and for whom”, not the adverb quoque, “also”, and the -que … -que pair simply links the two clauses. digni takes its complement in the ablative, caelesti numine. Magnus prints numine, “godhead”; the Latin Library prints munere, “gift” — on that reading what the two of them are called worthy of is a heavenly gift rather than divinity itself.

Four words of granting, and Jupiter hands Venus back her own verb: she said opto at 587, he says quod optas. cape is the imperative and the grant is made in it, with no formula of ratification. nata is the vocative of the perfect participle of nascor used as a noun — “born one”, hence “daughter”.

fatus erat is the pluperfect of for, fari, a deponent — passive in form, active in sense — and the tense sets the speech one step behind the narrative before the scene is handed to Venus. Two words, closed by a colon, are the whole of Jupiter's exit from the part.

sentences.t:
gaudet gratesque agit illa parenti,
perque leves auras iunctis invecta columbis
litus adit Laurens, ubi tectus harundine serpit
in freta flumineis vicina Numicius undis.
sentences.l: she rejoices and renders thanks to her parent, and, having ridden through the light breezes on yoked doves, she approaches the Laurentine shore, where, roofed over with reed, Numicius creeps with his river waters into the neighbouring sea.
sentences.i: she is glad and thanks her father, and, riding her yoked doves through the light air, she comes to the shore of Laurentum, where Numicius, hidden under reeds, glides with his river water into the sea close by.
sentences.n: The tense turns at gaudet: the pluperfect fatus erat gives way to a run of historic presents — gaudet, agit, adit, serpit, iubet, exsequitur, repurgat, respergit — which carries Venus' journey and the river's work until the perfect returns at restitit in 604. grates agere is the fixed phrase for rendering thanks. invecta is another middle participle — “having ridden in”, not “having been carried in” — and iunctis columbis is ablative: doves yoked to her car, the dove being Venus' bird. The Laurentine shore is the Latian coast; Numicius is the small river there, tectus harundine, “roofed with reed”. flumineis undis is an ablative of means standing beside in freta, an accusative of motion towards.

sentences.t:
Hunc iubet Aeneae, quaecumque obnoxia morti,
abluere et tacito deferre sub aequora cursu;
sentences.l: Him she bids wash away from Aeneas whatever things are liable to death, and carry them down beneath the waters in a silent current;
sentences.i: She orders the river to wash from Aeneas everything in him that is subject to death, and to carry it down under the sea in a noiseless current;
sentences.n: Hunc picks up Numicius, the second-to-last word of the line before — “him”, the river, not the shore. iubet takes an accusative with infinitives: hunc … abluere … deferre. Aeneae is a dative of the person something is taken from, which English turns into “from Aeneas”. quaecumque obnoxia morti is neuter plural with the verb “to be” left out, “whatever is liable to death” — everything mortal in him, not named more closely than that. tacito … cursu is an ablative of manner split open around deferre sub aequora.

sentences.t:
corniger exsequitur Veneris mandata suisque,
quidquid in Aenea fuerat mortale, repurgat
et respergit aquis:
sentences.l: the horn-bearer performs Venus' commands, and with his own waters purges out whatever in Aeneas had been mortal, and besprinkles him:
sentences.i: the horned god does what Venus commands: with his own waters he scours out everything in Aeneas that had been mortal, and washes him over:
sentences.n: corniger, “horn-bearer”, is the river-god himself: river gods are shown with a bull's horns, and Ovid names Numicius by the attribute instead of repeating the name. suisque stands at the end of 602 and waits for its noun until aquis, the third word of 604, with the mortal part of Aeneas enclosed between adjective and noun. in Aenea is the ablative of the Greek-declension name. fuerat is pluperfect — what had been mortal, before the washing. abluere at 601, repurgat here and respergit at 604 are three verbs of washing inside four lines, and lustratum at 605 closes the set: the vocabulary of the whole passage is that of purification, and no injury is named anywhere in it. Whether respergit takes the mortal remnant or Aeneas himself as its object the Latin leaves open. Magnus prints the present respergit; the Latin Library prints the perfect respersit, which would break the run of presents that began at 596.

sentences.l: the best part remained to him.
sentences.i: what was best in him stayed behind.
sentences.n: resto is “to be left over”, not “to stand firm”: what the current could not carry off is what is left. illi is a dative of the person concerned, so “was left to him” rather than a possessive. pars optima says without ceremony what the washing has separated — the part liable to death goes down the stream, the better part stays — and the four words, set off after a colon, are the point at which nothing mortal is left in him. The making of the god itself waits for Venus at 605-607, fecitque deum.

sentences.t:
Lustratum genetrix divino corpus odore
unxit et ambrosia cum dulci nectare mixta
contigit os fecitque deum, quem turba Quirini
nuncupat Indigetem temploque arisque recepit.
sentences.l: The purified body his mother anointed with divine fragrance, and touched his mouth with ambrosia mixed with sweet nectar, and made him a god, whom the throng of Quirinus calls Indiges and has received into both temple and altars.
sentences.i: His mother anointed the cleansed body with a divine perfume, touched his lips with ambrosia mingled with sweet nectar, and made him a god — the god the people of Quirinus call Indiges, and have taken into temple and altars.
sentences.n: Lustratum opens 605 and its noun corpus is the fourth word of the same line, with the subject genetrix set between them — lustro is the verb of ritual purification, so “the body, once purified”. genetrix, “she who bore him”, is Venus, and this is her last act here. ambrosia … mixta is ablative with cum dulci nectare inside it: the food and drink of the gods, put to the mouth to make a mortal immortal. turba Quirini is the Roman people, called after the name Romulus was given as a god. nuncupat takes two accusatives, “calls him Indiges”; Indiges is the cult title under which Aeneas was worshipped in Latium, and what the word itself meant was already disputed in antiquity. temploque arisque is the correlative -que … -que, “both … and”, a mannerism of high verse, and the two ablatives are the place he is received into, with no preposition.
